lessons.title: Printing in Java
objectives: print a line of text with System.out.println
stack several printed lines to build a screen
keep the cursor on the same line with System.out.print

steps.instruction: We are building a game title screen. How do we print something on it?
steps.code: System.out.println("*** DUNGEON QUEST ***");

points.label: System.out.println
points.text: This is the command that prints.

steps.keypoint: System.out.println("text"); prints a line.

steps.instruction: Look at the parts of the command.
steps.code: System.out.println("*** DUNGEON QUEST ***");

points.label: System.out.println
points.text: Capital S. Everything else is lowercase.
The message goes inside the brackets.
Text goes inside quotes. The quotes are not printed.
Ends the command.

steps.keypoint: Capital S on System. The message goes in the brackets, text goes in double quotes, and a semicolon ends the command.

steps.instruction: Change the title to your own.
steps.code: System.out.println("*** DUNGEON QUEST ***");
steps.hint: Change the text inside the quotes.
steps.after: Your game, your title.

steps.instruction: Each println starts a new line.

points.label: ln
points.text: The ln means: go to a new line after printing.

steps.keypoint: Each println starts a new line. That is what the ln means.

steps.instruction: Using print instead of println does not start a new line.

sides.label: print
sides.code:
System.out.print("Hi");
System.out.print("Bye");

sides.label: println
sides.code:
System.out.println("Hi");
System.out.println("Bye");

steps.keypoint: print does not start a new line. println does.

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.why: print does not end the line, so all three land on one line.
skills: keep the cursor on the same line with System.out.print

steps.instruction: Which of these really print in Java?
steps.why: Java only knows print and println, and only through System.out.
skills: print a line of text with System.out.println

steps.instruction: Fix this so it runs.
steps.code: System.out.println(Game over);
steps.solution: System.out.println("Game over");
steps.hint: Text needs quotes around it.
steps.after: Without quotes, Java reads Game and over as code.
skills: print a line of text with System.out.println

steps.instruction: Print these two lines exactly.
steps.code:
// line 1: My name is Ada.
// line 2: I like comedy.
steps.target:
My name is Ada.
I like comedy.
steps.solution:
System.out.println("My name is Ada.");
System.out.println("I like comedy.");
steps.hint: One println per line. Copy the text exactly.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.1.5, Welcome Program.
skills: stack several printed lines to build a screen

steps.hint: Three printlns. The two spaces before 1. go inside the quotes.
steps.after: You built the screen you started with.

lessons.title: Variables and Types
objectives: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name
use = to put a value in, and change it later
choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: We are building a player card. How do we store the values it needs?
body: We need somewhere to keep the values.
A variable is a box that holds one value.
steps.keypoint: A variable is a box that holds one value.

steps.instruction: Every variable has three parts.
steps.code: int level = 5;

points.label: int
points.text: The type. What kind of value the box can hold.

points.label: level
points.text: The name. What you call the box.
The value. What goes in the box.

steps.keypoint: Every variable has a type, a name and a value: int level = 5;

steps.instruction: Declaring makes the box.
steps.code: int level;
body: Write the type, then a name.
The box is empty until you put something in.
steps.keypoint: Declaring makes the box: int level;

steps.instruction: Initializing makes the box and fills it.
steps.code: int level = 5;
body: The = puts the value into the box.
Most of the time you do both at once, like this.
steps.keypoint: Initializing makes the box and fills it: int level = 5;

steps.instruction: Assigning changes the value.
body: The box already exists, so you do not write the type again.
The old value is gone.
steps.keypoint: Assigning changes the value with no type: level = 0;

steps.instruction: Fix this so it runs.
steps.hint: The box goes on the left. The value goes on the right.
steps.after: Read it as: put the right side into the left side.
skills: use = to put a value in, and change it later
steps.keypoint: The box goes on the left of the =. The value goes on the right.

steps.instruction: Primitive type: int holds whole numbers.
body: -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3. No decimal point.
Use it to count things.
steps.code: int level = 7;
steps.keypoint: int holds whole numbers, used to count.

steps.instruction: Primitive type: double holds numbers with decimals.
body: Use it to measure things.
steps.code: double health = 2.5;
steps.keypoint: double holds numbers with decimals.

steps.instruction: Primitive type: boolean holds true or false.
body: Nothing else fits in the box.
steps.code: boolean online = true;
steps.keypoint: boolean holds only true or false.

steps.instruction: Primitive type: char holds a single character.
body: One letter, one digit or one symbol.
steps.code: char rank = 'A';

points.text: A char goes in single quotes.

steps.keypoint: char holds one character, in single quotes.

steps.instruction: Which type holds each value?
steps.why: 5.0 is a double. The decimal point decides it.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: String holds text of any length.
body: String is not a primitive type.
steps.code: String name = "Ada";

points.label: String
points.text: Capital S.
Text goes in double quotes.

steps.keypoint: String is not a primitive type. Capital S, double quotes.

steps.instruction: Fix this so it runs.
steps.code:
String name = 'Ada';
System.out.println(name);
steps.solution:
String name = "Ada";
System.out.println(name);
steps.hint: Single quotes hold one character. Text needs double quotes.
steps.after: 'A' is a char. "A" is a String.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: There are a few rules when naming variables.

rules.text: The name must start with a letter, $ or _
The rest can have letters, numbers or _
Names are case sensitive
rules.example: player and Player are two different boxes

rules.text: Write names in lowerCamelCase: start lowercase, then a capital for each new word

steps.keypoint: Names start with a letter, $ or _, are case sensitive, and are written in lowerCamelCase.

steps.instruction: Sort these variable names.
steps.why: A space or a hyphen splits the name in two. A name cannot start with a number. x is legal, but it tells the next reader nothing.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: Give each value the right type.
steps.hint: Look at each value. Quotes, a decimal point, or true and false all give it away.
steps.after: The value decides the type.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.why: a = b copies what is in b into a. The value moves right to left.
skills: use = to put a value in, and change it later

steps.instruction: Fix this so it runs.
steps.code:
int Level = 7;
System.out.println(level);
steps.solution:
int level = 7;
System.out.println(level);
steps.hint: Java sees Level and level as two different boxes.
steps.after: Names are case sensitive. Only one box was ever made.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: Match each type to a value it can hold.
steps.why: The quotes tell you most of it. Double quotes mean String, single quotes mean char.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Fill in your own values to make your card.
steps.hint: Match each value to the type in front of it. Text needs double quotes, a char needs single ones.
steps.after: Five boxes, five types, one card.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

lessons.title: User Input
objectives: read what the user types with readLine
choose the reader that matches the type you need
store a typed value in a variable and use it later

steps.instruction: Your player card always says Ada. How do we ask the player for their own name?
body: A real game asks the player who they are.
We need a way to get a value from whoever is playing.
steps.code: String name = "Ada";
steps.keypoint: readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean get a value from the player.

steps.instruction: Java gives us four readers, one for each type.

rules.text: readLine hands back a String
readInt hands back an int
readDouble hands back a double
readBoolean hands back a boolean

steps.keypoint: There is one reader per type, and the box in front must match it.

steps.instruction: Every one of them works the same way.
steps.code: String name = readLine("Your name? ");

points.label: "Your name? "
points.text: The question goes inside the brackets.

points.label: String name =
points.text: The answer comes back and goes into the box.

steps.keypoint: The prompt goes inside the brackets, and the answer comes back into a variable.

steps.instruction: Run it, then type a name when it asks.
steps.code:
String name = readLine("Your name? ");
System.out.println("Welcome, " + name + "!");
steps.after: It printed the question, waited for you, then used your answer.

steps.instruction: readInt hands back a whole number you can calculate with.
body: readLine would hand back text. Adding 1 to the text "7" gives "71".
steps.code:
int level = readInt("Starting level? ");
System.out.println("Next level is " + (level + 1));

steps.instruction: Run it and type a whole number.
steps.code:
int level = readInt("Starting level? ");
System.out.println("Next level is " + (level + 1));
steps.after: It added 1 to your number, because a number came back.

steps.instruction: Run it and type a number with a decimal point.
steps.code:
double health = readDouble("Health? ");
System.out.println("Half of that is " + (health / 2));
steps.after: readDouble keeps the decimal part.

steps.instruction: Run it and type true or false.
steps.code:
boolean online = readBoolean("Online? ");
System.out.println("Online: " + online);
steps.after: Four questions, four readers.

steps.instruction: Match each reader to the type it hands back.
steps.why: The reader decides the type, and the box in front has to match it.
skills: choose the reader that matches the type you need

steps.instruction: Ask for the player name, then greet them.
steps.code: // ask "Name? " and print:  Hi, <name>
steps.solution:
String name = readLine("Name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name);
steps.hint: Store what readLine hands back, then use that box in the println.
steps.after: The prompt Name? was printed by readLine, not by you.
skills: read what the user types with readLine

steps.instruction: Ask for an age, then say what it will be next year.
steps.code: // ask "Age? " and print:  Next year you are <age+1>
steps.solution:
int age = readInt("Age? ");
System.out.println("Next year you are " + (age + 1));
steps.hint: An age is a whole number, so use the reader that hands one back.
steps.after: readLine would have given you "16" and printed 161.
skills: choose the reader that matches the type you need

steps.instruction: Ask for a price, then print double it.
steps.code: // ask "Price? " and print:  Two of those cost <price*2>
steps.solution:
double price = readDouble("Price? ");
System.out.println("Two of those cost " + (price * 2));
steps.hint: A price has a decimal point.
steps.after: A double stays a double through the multiplication.
skills: choose the reader that matches the type you need

steps.instruction: Fix this so it runs.
steps.solution:
String name = readLine("Your name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name);
steps.hint: The question belongs inside the brackets of readLine.
steps.after: readLine prints the question itself. You never print it separately.
skills: read what the user types with readLine

steps.instruction: Ask the player for a name, a level and health, then print the card.
steps.target:
Name? Ada
Level? 7
Health? 2.5
Name: Ada
Level: 7
Health: 2.5
steps.hint: Three readers, then three printlns. One space after each colon.
steps.after: The card is filled in by whoever is playing, not by you.
skills: store a typed value in a variable and use it later

lessons.title: Arithmetic Expressions
objectives: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
predict the result of whole-number division
use the remainder operator to find what is left over

steps.instruction: We are building a calculator. How do we make Java do the maths?
body: A calculator takes numbers and works something out.
Java does the maths for us.

steps.instruction: Adding two variables.
body: The + works out the answer, then println shows it.
steps.keypoint: Java works out + - * / and % for you.

steps.instruction: A calculator asks for the numbers instead.
body: Same two lines of maths. The values now come from whoever is using it.

steps.instruction: Run it and type two numbers.
steps.after: That is a working calculator. Now we give it the rest of the operations.

steps.instruction: Java has five arithmetic operators.

rules.text: + adds
- subtracts
* multiplies
/ divides
% gives the remainder

steps.keypoint: The five arithmetic operators are + - * / and %.

steps.instruction: Run it and see all five.
steps.after: Two of those look wrong. 12 / 5 gave 2, and % gave 2 as well.

steps.instruction: % gives you what is left over.
body: Share 12 sweets between 5 people.
Each person gets 2, and 2 sweets are left over.
12 / 5 is the 2 each. 12 % 5 is the 2 left over.
steps.code:
System.out.println(12 / 5);
System.out.println(12 % 5);
steps.keypoint: % gives the remainder. x % 2 is 0 for even and 1 for odd.

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.code: System.out.println(20 % 6);
steps.why: 6 goes into 20 three times, which is 18. 20 - 18 leaves 2.
skills: use the remainder operator to find what is left over

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.code:
System.out.println(9 % 2);
System.out.println(10 % 2);
steps.why: x % 2 is 1 for an odd number and 0 for an even one. This is how you test whether a number is even.
skills: use the remainder operator to find what is left over

steps.instruction: Shortcuts for changing a number you already have.

rules.text: ++ adds one
rules.example: score++   is the same as   score = score + 1

rules.text: -- takes one away
rules.example: lives--   is the same as   lives = lives - 1

rules.text: += adds an amount
rules.example: score += 10   is the same as   score = score + 10

rules.text: -= takes an amount away
rules.example: hp -= 3   is the same as   hp = hp - 3

rules.text: *= and /= work the same way
rules.example: gold *= 2   is the same as   gold = gold * 2

steps.keypoint: ++ and -- change a number by one. += -= *= /= change it by an amount.

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.why: 10 plus 5 is 15, then ++ adds one more.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations

steps.instruction: Use a shortcut to take 3 off hp, then print it.
steps.code:
int hp = 20;
// take 3 off hp using a shortcut, then print hp
steps.hint: The shortcut for hp = hp - 3.
steps.after: hp -= 3 and hp = hp - 3 do exactly the same thing.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations

steps.instruction: Java does maths in the order you learned at school.

rules.text: Brackets first
Then * / and %
Then + and -
Same level goes left to right

steps.keypoint: Brackets first, then * / %, then + -, left to right at the same level.

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.code: System.out.println(2 + 3 * 4);
steps.why: 3 * 4 happens first, giving 12, then 2 is added. Brackets would change it: (2 + 3) * 4 is 20.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations

steps.instruction: Two whole numbers divided give a whole number.
body: Java throws the .5 away. It does not round to the nearest.
This is called truncation.
steps.code: System.out.println(7 / 2);
steps.keypoint: Two whole numbers divided give a whole number. 7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5.

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.code: System.out.println(9 / 10);
steps.why: 10 goes into 9 zero times, so the answer is 0. Everything after the point is thrown away, however close it was.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division

steps.instruction: One double anywhere makes the answer a double.
body: 7.0 is a double, so Java keeps the decimal part.
You only need one of the two numbers to be a double.
steps.keypoint: One double anywhere makes the answer a double.

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.why: b is a double, so the division keeps the decimal part.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.code:
double half = 7 / 2;
System.out.println(half);
steps.why: 7 / 2 is worked out FIRST, and both are whole numbers, so it gives 3. Storing 3 in a double only makes it 3.0. The decimal was lost before the box ever saw it.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division
steps.keypoint: double half = 7 / 2; gives 3.0. The division finished before the box saw it.

steps.instruction: Project: a fair share calculator.
body: Ask how many coins and how many players.
Print how many each player gets, and how many are left over.
steps.target:
Coins? 17
Players? 5
Each gets: 3
Left over: 2
steps.hint: / gives the share each. % gives what is left. Keep the maths in brackets inside the println.
steps.after: 17 coins between 5 players is 3 each with 2 spare. / and % answer the two halves of the same question.
skills: predict the result of whole-number division
use the remainder operator to find what is left over

steps.instruction: Project: turning seconds into hours, minutes and seconds.
body: 3661 seconds is 1 hour, 1 minute and 1 second.
Each step uses / to take out the whole units, then % to keep what is left.

rules.text: Hours: divide by 3600
What is left after the hours
Minutes: divide what is left by 60
Seconds: what is left after the minutes

steps.instruction: Now write it. Ask for a number of seconds and break it up.
steps.hint: Store what is left over in its own box after the hours, then split that into minutes and seconds.
steps.after: Every unit conversion works this way: / takes the whole units out, % keeps the remainder for the next step.
skills: use the remainder operator to find what is left over
predict the result of whole-number division

lessons.title: Casting
objectives: use (double) so whole-number division keeps its decimal
use (int) to turn a decimal into a whole number
round to the nearest whole number using casting

steps.instruction: Two whole numbers divided give a whole number. How do we keep the decimal part?
steps.code:
System.out.println(7 / 2);
System.out.println(7.0 / 2);
body: Two whole numbers give a whole number.
So we need a way to turn a number into a double on purpose.

steps.instruction: A cast tells Java to treat a value as another type.
steps.code:
int a = 7;
System.out.println((double) a / 2);

points.label: (double)
points.text: Treat a as a double, just for this line.

steps.keypoint: A cast tells Java to treat a value as another type: (double) a / 2

steps.instruction: The two directions are not the same.

rules.text: int to double happens on its own, because nothing is lost
double to int needs a cast, because the decimal part is thrown away
(int) chops. It never rounds

steps.keypoint: int to double happens on its own. double to int needs a cast, and (int) chops rather than rounds.

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.code: System.out.println((int) 9.99);
steps.why: (int) throws away everything after the point, however close it was to the next number.
skills: use (int) to turn a decimal into a whole number

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.code: System.out.println((double) (7 / 2));
steps.why: The brackets make 7 / 2 happen first, so it is 3 before the cast ever sees it. Casting afterwards only makes it 3.0. The cast has to reach a number BEFORE the division.
skills: use (double) so whole-number division keeps its decimal

steps.instruction: Use it to stop division truncating.
body: 7 XP out of 20 is 35 percent.
Without the cast the division finishes first and gives 0.
steps.keypoint: Cast before dividing to keep the decimal part.

steps.instruction: Print what 3 out of 8 is as a percentage.
steps.hint: Cast the first number before the division happens.
steps.after: Without the cast, 3 / 8 is 0 and the answer is 0.0.
skills: use (double) so whole-number division keeps its decimal

steps.instruction: Use it to round, by nudging first.
body: (int) always chops down.
Adding 0.5 first turns chopping into rounding.
steps.keypoint: Add 0.5 then cast to int to round to the nearest whole number.

steps.instruction: Make this round to the nearest whole number.
steps.code:
double rating = 4.7;
System.out.println((int) (rating + ⟦1⟧));
steps.hint: Anything at .5 or above should tip over to the next whole number.
steps.after: 4.7 plus 0.5 is 5.2, and chopping that gives 5.
skills: round to the nearest whole number using casting

steps.instruction: An int is 32 bits, so it cannot hold every number.
body: There is a largest int and a smallest one.
Java will tell you what they are.
steps.code:
System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE);
System.out.println(Integer.MIN_VALUE);
steps.keypoint: An int is 32 bits, so it has a largest and smallest value.

steps.instruction: Go past the top and it wraps round to the bottom.
body: This is called overflow.
Java does not warn you. It just keeps counting from the other end.
steps.code: System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1);
steps.keypoint: Going past the top wraps round to the bottom. That is overflow, and Java gives no warning.

steps.instruction: Run it and watch a number go wrong.
steps.after: It counted up, hit the ceiling, and came back at the floor.

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.why: One past the top lands on the bottom, and the second step moves one up from there.
skills: use (int) to turn a decimal into a whole number

steps.instruction: Project: round a film rating to the nearest whole star.
steps.code:
// ask "Rating? " with readDouble
// then print:  Stars: <rating rounded>
steps.solution:
double rating = readDouble("Rating? ");
System.out.println("Stars: " + (int) (rating + 0.5));
steps.hint: Add 0.5, then cast to int. Keep the whole sum in brackets.
steps.after: 4.6 rounds up to 5. A rating of 4.4 would give 4.
skills: round to the nearest whole number using casting

steps.instruction: Project: print a test score as a percentage, rounded.
steps.code:
// ask "Correct? " and "Total? " with readInt
// then print:  Score: <percent rounded>%
steps.hint: Cast before dividing to keep the decimal, then add 0.5 and cast to int to round.
steps.after: Both casts were needed. One kept the decimal, the other rounded it.
skills: use (double) so whole-number division keeps its decimal
round to the nearest whole number using casting

lessons.title: Booleans
objectives: create boolean variables that hold true or false
tell a boolean apart from text, a character and a number
read a true/false answer from the user

steps.instruction: A game has to remember facts that are simply yes or no. How do we store one?
steps.code:
boolean alive = true;
System.out.println(alive);
body: Use it for any fact that is a yes or a no.
steps.keypoint: A boolean holds true or false and nothing else.

steps.instruction: Games are full of them.

rules.text: Is the player alive?
Is the door unlocked?
Is the sound on?

steps.instruction: Run the status panel.
steps.after: Three facts, three booleans.

steps.instruction: Change one the same way you change any variable.
body: No type the second time, because the box already exists.

steps.instruction: Which of these is really a boolean?
steps.why: "true" in double quotes is a String. Java is also case sensitive, so True is not the keyword true.
skills: tell a boolean apart from text, a character and a number
steps.keypoint: "true" in quotes is a String, and True is not the keyword.

steps.instruction: Fix this so it runs.
steps.code:
boolean alive = "true";
System.out.println(alive);
steps.solution:
boolean alive = true;
System.out.println(alive);
steps.hint: The quotes make it text. A boolean wants the keyword.
steps.after: true and "true" both print as true, which is exactly why the mistake is easy to miss.
skills: tell a boolean apart from text, a character and a number

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.why: The second line replaced the value. A box holds one thing at a time.
skills: create boolean variables that hold true or false

steps.instruction: You can ask the player directly.
steps.code:
boolean ready = readBoolean("Ready? ");
System.out.println("Ready: " + ready);
body: They type the word true or the word false.

steps.instruction: Run it and type true or false.
steps.code:
boolean ready = readBoolean("Ready? ");
System.out.println("Ready: " + ready);
steps.after: readBoolean hands back a real boolean, not text.

steps.instruction: Ask whether they like ice cream, then print the answer.
steps.code: // ask "Do you like ice cream? " and print:  You said: <answer>
steps.target:
Do you like ice cream? true
You said: true
steps.solution:
boolean likes = readBoolean("Do you like ice cream? ");
System.out.println("You said: " + likes);
steps.hint: Store what readBoolean hands back, then print that box.
steps.after: A boolean travels from the keyboard into a box and out again.
skills: read a true/false answer from the user

lessons.title: Logical Operators
objectives: combine two booleans with && so both must be true
combine two booleans with || so either will do
flip a boolean with !

steps.instruction: A dungeon door needs a key and enough strength. How do we join two conditions together?

rules.text: ! reverses a boolean
|| is true when at least one side is true
&& is true only when both sides are true

steps.keypoint: Logical operators connect and modify boolean expressions.

steps.instruction: ! reverses the boolean.
steps.code:
boolean alive = true;
System.out.println(!alive);
body: Read it as "not".
steps.keypoint: ! reverses a boolean.

steps.instruction: Fill in what ! gives.
steps.why: ! always gives the opposite of what it was handed.
skills: flip a boolean with !

steps.instruction: || is true when at least one side is true.
body: Read it as "or". Either one will do.
steps.keypoint: || is true when at least one side is true.

steps.instruction: Fill in what || gives.
steps.why: Only one row is false, the one where neither side is true.
skills: combine two booleans with || so either will do

steps.instruction: && is true only when both sides are true.
body: Read it as "and". Both must hold.
steps.keypoint: && is true only when both sides are true.

steps.instruction: Fill in what && gives.
steps.why: Only one row is true, the one where both sides are.
skills: combine two booleans with && so both must be true

steps.instruction: A dungeon door needs the key and the strength.
body: && because one without the other is not enough.

steps.instruction: Run it, then change strong to false and run it again.
steps.after: With && , one false shuts the door.

steps.instruction: A shop takes gold or gems.
body: || because either payment works.

steps.instruction: An alarm sounds when the player is NOT hidden.
steps.code:
boolean hidden = false;

lessons.title: Comparison Operators
objectives: compare two numbers and get a boolean back
tell == apart from =

steps.instruction: We are building the gates that let a player through. How do we ask Java whether one value beats another?
body: A gate needs a yes or a no.
Comparison operators turn two numbers into a boolean.

steps.instruction: There are six of them.

rules.text: == is equal to
!= is not equal to
> is greater than
< is less than
>= is greater than or equal to
<= is less than or equal to

steps.keypoint: The six comparison operators are == != > < >= and <=.

steps.instruction: Run it and see all six.
steps.after: Every one of them gave back true or false.

steps.instruction: == asks a question. = puts a value in.
steps.code:
int hp = 5;
System.out.println(hp == 5);
body: One equals sign stores. Two equals signs compare.
Mixing them up is the commonest mistake in this lesson.
steps.keypoint: One = stores a value. Two == ask a question.

steps.instruction: Fix this so it runs.
steps.code:
int hp = 5;
System.out.println(hp = 5);
steps.solution:
int hp = 5;
System.out.println(hp == 5);
steps.hint: The line should ask a question, not store a value.
steps.after: One = assigns. Two == compare.
skills: compare two numbers and get a boolean back

steps.instruction: These work on primitive types.
body: int, double, char and boolean can all be compared this way.
String is not a primitive type, so == does not compare its text. That comes later.
steps.keypoint: Comparison operators work on primitive types. String needs .equals().

steps.instruction: Does each comparison give true or false?
steps.why: >= and <= let the two sides be equal. > and < do not.
skills: compare two numbers and get a boolean back

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.why: >= allows equal, so the first is true. > needs strictly more, so the second is false.
skills: compare two numbers and get a boolean back

steps.instruction: Build a gate: the player passes when their level is at least 5.
steps.code:

// print:  Pass: <true or false>

System.out.println("Pass: " + (level >= 5));
steps.hint: "At least 5" means 5 counts, so it is not the plain greater-than.
steps.after: Level 5 passes. Level 4 would not.
skills: compare two numbers and get a boolean back

steps.instruction: Build a gate: the door opens when the player is NOT out of keys.
steps.code:
int keys = 2;
// print:  Open: <true or false>
steps.solution:
int keys = 2;
System.out.println("Open: " + (keys != 0));
steps.hint: Out of keys means keys is 0.
steps.after: != 0 reads as "has at least one".
skills: compare two numbers and get a boolean back

steps.instruction: Build a gate: they ride when they are tall enough and old enough.
steps.hint: Two comparisons joined with && from the last lesson.
steps.after: Comparisons make the booleans, and && joins them.
skills: compare two numbers and get a boolean back

It does not work for a thousand.

steps.code: // print * four times, one per line

rules.text: The first part makes the counter and runs once
The second part is checked before every pass
The third part runs after every pass

skills: work out how many times a loop body runs

lessons.title: While Loops
objectives: stop a while loop by changing the condition inside it
choose between a for loop and a while loop

steps.instruction: We want to keep attacking the boss until its health runs out. How do we repeat something when we do not know the number of times?
body: A for loop needs a count before it starts.
Nobody knows how many hits the boss will take.

steps.instruction: A while loop repeats for as long as a condition stays true.
steps.output:
Boss hp 3
Boss hp 2
Boss hp 1
body: It checks the condition, runs the body, then checks again.
steps.keypoint: A while loop repeats for as long as its condition stays true.

steps.instruction: Step through it and watch the condition decide.

frames.note: Is 3 greater than 0? Yes, so run the body.
Is 2 greater than 0? Yes, go round again.
Is 1 greater than 0? Yes, once more.

frames.out:
Boss hp 3
Boss hp 2
Boss hp 1

Boss hp 3
Boss hp 2
Boss hp 1

frames.note: Is 0 greater than 0? No. The loop stops.
frames.out:
Boss hp 3
Boss hp 2
Boss hp 1

steps.instruction: A while loop has two jobs you must do yourself.

rules.text: Set the variable up before the loop
Change it inside the loop, or the condition never turns false

steps.keypoint: Set the variable up before the loop, and change it inside, or it never ends.

steps.instruction: Forget to change it and the loop never ends.
body: hp stays 3 forever, so the condition stays true forever.
This is an infinite loop. The program never finishes and never gets to the code below it.
Do not run this one. Every while loop needs something inside it that moves towards stopping.
steps.keypoint: A loop whose condition never turns false is an infinite loop. It never reaches the code below it.

steps.instruction: This loop never ends. Tap the line that should have changed.
steps.why: The body only prints. Nothing takes anything off count, so it stays 5 and the condition stays true. A count-- belongs on this line.
skills: stop a while loop by changing the condition inside it

steps.instruction: Both count to 3. Pick the one that fits what you know.

sides.label: for
while

steps.instruction: Which loop suits each job?

items.text: Print all 5 items in a list
Keep asking until the player types the right password
Halve a number until it reaches 1

steps.why: Use a for loop when you know the count before you start. Use a while loop when the stopping point depends on something that happens along the way.
skills: choose between a for loop and a while loop
steps.keypoint: Use for when you know the count. Use while when you do not.

steps.instruction: What comes out?
steps.why: 8, then 4, then 2. Next n becomes 1, and 1 is not greater than 1, so it stops before printing it.
skills: stop a while loop by changing the condition inside it

steps.instruction: Type a while loop that counts down from 5 to 1.
steps.code: // print 5 4 3 2 1, one per line, using a while loop

steps.after: The n-- is what lets it finish.
skills: stop a while loop by changing the condition inside it

steps.hint: Keep going while n is 100 or less, and double it each pass.
steps.after: 128 was over 100, so the loop stopped before printing it.
skills: choose between a for loop and a while loop

lessons.title: If Statements
objectives: run a block of code only when a condition is true
use else to handle the other case
use the remainder operator inside a condition

steps.instruction: So far our gates only print true or false. How do we make the program act on the answer?
steps.code:
boolean canOpen = true;
System.out.println("Door opens: " + canOpen);
body: Printing the answer is not the same as using it.
A real game opens the door, or does not.

steps.instruction: if runs a block only when the condition is true.
steps.output:
The door swings open.
You walk on.

points.label: if (hasKey)
points.text: The condition goes in round brackets.
Only the lines inside are skipped when it is false.

steps.keypoint: if runs a block only when its condition is true.

steps.instruction: else covers the other case.
body: Exactly one block runs. Never both, and never neither.
steps.keypoint: else covers the other case. Exactly one block runs.

steps.instruction: Step through it and watch Java choose.

frames.note: So this line is skipped entirely.
The if is finished. Only one of the two blocks ever ran.

steps.instruction: hp is exactly 0. What comes out?
steps.why: 0 is not greater than 0, so the condition is false and else runs. Use >= 0 if zero should count as standing.
skills: use else to handle the other case

steps.instruction: else if checks the next thing only when the last one failed.
body: Java stops at the first condition that is true.
Order matters. Put >= 80 first and every score above 90 would print B as well.
steps.keypoint: else if is checked only when the ones above it failed, and the first match wins.

steps.instruction: A remainder makes a good condition.
body: n % 2 is 0 for an even number and 1 for an odd one.
So n % 2 == 0 asks whether n is even.
steps.keypoint: if (n % 2 == 0) asks whether n is even.

steps.instruction: 8 is even, but this says odd. Fix it.
steps.hint: An even number leaves nothing behind when you divide it by 2.
steps.after: 8 % 2 is 0, so the condition has to test against 0.
skills: use the remainder operator inside a condition

steps.instruction: This prints the line even when it should not. Tap the line to blame.
steps.why: The semicolon right after the brackets ends the if there and then. The block below it is no longer attached to anything, so it always runs.
skills: run a block of code only when a condition is true
steps.keypoint: A semicolon straight after the brackets ends the if, so the block below always runs.

steps.instruction: Print Pass when the score is 50 or more, and Fail otherwise.
steps.code:
int score = 64;
// print Pass or Fail
steps.hint: One if, one else. 50 itself should pass.
steps.after: >= let 50 through. > would have failed it.
skills: use else to handle the other case

steps.instruction: Ask for a number, then say whether it is even or odd.
steps.code:
// ask "Number? " with readInt
// then print even or odd
steps.hint: Read the number, then test the remainder.
steps.after: The same test works for any number they type.
skills: use the remainder operator inside a condition

steps.instruction: Ask for a mark, then print A, B or C.
steps.code:
// ask "Mark? " with readInt
// 90 or more is A, 80 or more is B, anything else is C
steps.hint: Check the highest grade first, or 95 would come out as B.
steps.after: First match wins, so the order of the tests is part of the answer.
skills: use else to handle the other case

lessons.title: Loop-and-a-Half
objectives: use break to leave a loop from the middle
write a while (true) loop that asks once and checks once
stop a loop on a sentinel value

steps.instruction: We are building a number guessing game. How do we keep asking until the player gets it right?
body: The game has to ask, then check, then ask again.
We do not know how many guesses it will take.

steps.instruction: A plain while loop makes you ask the question twice.
body: One readInt above the loop, because while checks before it runs.
Another inside, to get the next guess.
The same question written on two lines is easy to get out of step.

steps.instruction: while (true) never stops on its own. break is the way out.

points.label: while (true)
points.text: The condition is always true, so the loop cannot end by itself.

points.label: break;
points.text: Leaves the loop at once, skipping the rest of the body.

steps.keypoint: while (true) runs forever, and break is the way out.

steps.instruction: Step through two guesses and watch break end it.

frames.note: The condition is true, so the body runs.
Ask for a guess. The player types 4.
Is 4 equal to 6? No, so skip the block.
Back to the top. The condition is still true.
Ask again. This time the player types 6.
Is 6 equal to 6? Yes, so run the block.
break leaves the loop. Try again! below is never reached.

steps.instruction: This shape has a name: ask, check, act.

rules.text: Ask at the top of the loop
Check in the middle, and break when you are done
Act at the bottom, only when you did not break

steps.keypoint: The shape is ask at the top, check in the middle and break, act at the bottom.

steps.instruction: Tap the only line that can end this loop.
steps.why: while (true) is never false, so nothing at the top can stop it. Only break gets you out.
skills: use break to leave a loop from the middle

steps.instruction: A sentinel is a value that means stop.
steps.output:
Number (0 to stop): 5
Number (0 to stop): 7
Number (0 to stop): 0
12
body: The prompt says what the sentinel is, so the player is not guessing.
Pick a value that cannot be real data.
steps.keypoint: A sentinel is the value that ends the loop. Say what it is in the prompt.

steps.instruction: Fill in the statement that leaves the loop.
steps.hint: One statement ends a loop early.
steps.after: Without it, count would keep rising forever.
skills: use break to leave a loop from the middle

steps.instruction: Keep asking for a number until they type 0, then print how many they gave.
steps.code:
// ask "Number (0 to stop): " until they type 0
// then print how many numbers they typed before the 0
steps.target:
Number (0 to stop): 4
Number (0 to stop): 9
Number (0 to stop): 2
Number (0 to stop): 0
3
steps.hint: Break before you count, so the 0 itself is not counted.
steps.after: The 0 ended the loop without joining the total.
skills: stop a loop on a sentinel value

steps.instruction: Build the guessing game. The secret number is 6.
steps.target:
Guess? 3
Try again!
Guess? 8
Try again!
Guess? 6
Correct!
steps.hint: Ask at the top, check in the middle and break, print Try again at the bottom.
steps.after: That is the loop-and-a-half, and it is the shape the exam asks for.
skills: write a while (true) loop that asks once and checks once

lessons.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation
objectives: explain why the right-hand side of && or || is sometimes skipped
put a guard on the left so the right side is safe
work out which side of an expression actually runs

steps.instruction: Dividing by zero crashes the program. How do we check a value before we use it?
body: This is the obvious way to work out an average.
With hits at 0 it does not give 0. It crashes.

steps.instruction: && stops at the first false, so the division never happens.
body: hits != 0 is false. Once one side of && is false the answer is false whatever the other side says.
So Java never looks at the right side, and the division never runs.
This is not a speed trick. It is the only reason the program survives.
steps.keypoint: && stops at the first false, so the right side is never worked out.

steps.instruction: Fill in what && gives.
steps.why: Both rows starting false are already decided. Java stops there.
skills: work out which side of an expression actually runs

steps.instruction: || stops at the first true, for the same reason.
body: hits == 0 is true, so the answer is true whatever follows.
The division on the right is skipped.
steps.keypoint: || stops at the first true, for the same reason.

steps.instruction: The guard has to go on the left.

rules.text: Java always reads the left side first
Put the check first and the risky part is protected
rules.example: safe, because the check runs before the division

rules.text: Put it second and the crash happens before the check

steps.keypoint: Put the guard on the left, or the crash happens before the check.

steps.instruction: 5 / 0 would crash. Does this?
steps.code:
int n = 0;
System.out.println(n != 0 && 5 / n > 1);
steps.why: n != 0 is false, so && gives up immediately and the division is never reached.
skills: explain why the right-hand side of && or || is sometimes skipped

steps.instruction: Pick the operator that keeps this safe.
steps.code:
int n = 0;
System.out.println(n == 0 ⟦1⟧ 10 / n > 1);
steps.hint: n == 0 is true here. Which operator gives up as soon as it sees a true?
steps.after: && would have carried on to the division and crashed.
skills: put a guard on the left so the right side is safe

steps.instruction: Print the average safely, or 0 when there were no hits.
steps.hint: Check hits before you divide by it.
steps.after: Guarding with an if works too. Short-circuiting is the same idea inside one expression.
skills: put a guard on the left so the right side is safe

steps.instruction: Ask for two numbers, then say whether the first divides evenly by the second without crashing.
steps.hint: Put the d != 0 check on the left of &&.
steps.after: The guard on the left is what stops the remainder ever being worked out.
skills: put a guard on the left so the right side is safe

lessons.title: De Morgan's Laws
objectives: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not
rewrite !(a || b) without the outer not
check that two boolean expressions mean the same thing

steps.instruction: You get in with a key and enough strength. How do we write the condition for being turned away?
body: Putting a ! in front works, and it reads as a double negative.
There is a way to say the same thing without the outer not.

steps.instruction: not (A and B) is the same as (not A) or (not B).
body: The ! moves onto each part, and the && flips to ||.
"Not both" means "at least one is missing".
steps.keypoint: !(A && B) is the same as !A || !B.

steps.instruction: Check the law on every combination.
steps.why: The two columns are identical on every row, which is what makes it a law.
skills: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not

steps.instruction: not (A or B) is the same as (not A) and (not B).
body: Same recipe. The ! moves onto each part, and this time the || flips to &&.
"Neither" means "not this and not that".
steps.keypoint: !(A || B) is the same as !A && !B.

steps.instruction: The operator must flip. That is the part people forget.

rules.text: !(A && B) becomes !A || !B
!(A || B) becomes !A && !B
Leaving the operator alone gives a different answer
rules.example: !A && !B is not the same as !(A && B)

steps.keypoint: The ! moves onto each part AND the operator flips.

steps.instruction: a is true and b is false. What comes out?
steps.why: !a is false and !b is true, so the || gives true. It matches !(a && b), which is also true.
skills: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not

steps.instruction: Rewrite !(a && b) without the outer brackets.
steps.hint: The && inside the brackets has to flip.
steps.after: && would have given false, which is the wrong answer.
skills: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not

steps.instruction: Print whether the player is turned away, in De Morgan form.
steps.hint: ! on each part, and flip the && to ||.
steps.after: No outer bracket, and it reads as "no key, or not strong enough".
skills: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not

steps.instruction: Ask for an age and a height, then say who is turned away from the ride.
steps.hint: The opposite of >= 10 is < 10, and the && flips to ||.
steps.after: Flipping each comparison is the same move as putting a ! on each part.
skills: rewrite !(a && b) without the outer not

lessons.title: Strings
objectives: compare Strings with .equals()
explain why == is the wrong way to compare text
join Strings together with +

steps.instruction: A gate should open only when the player types the magic word. How do we compare two pieces of text?
body: Numbers are easy to compare. Text is not.
First we need to know what a String really is.

steps.instruction: A String is a sequence of characters in double quotes.
body: With no quotes, Java prints what is inside the box.
With quotes, it prints the four letters w o r d.
steps.keypoint: A String is a sequence of characters in double quotes.

steps.instruction: A String is not a primitive type.

rules.text: The primitive types are int, double, char and boolean
String is not one of them
It starts with a capital S, which is how Java writes an object

steps.keypoint: String is not a primitive type. The capital S means it is an object.

steps.instruction: That capital letter matters more than it looks.
body: A capital S means String is an object rather than a plain value.
You will meet objects properly later in the course.
For now, one thing follows from it, and it is the whole point of this lesson.

steps.instruction: Joining two Strings is called concatenation.
body: The + sign glues them into one String.
Nothing is added up. The characters are placed end to end.
steps.keypoint: Concatenation joins Strings with +. Spaces are yours to add.

steps.instruction: Java joins exactly what you give it, so spaces are yours to add.
body: The space has to be a String of its own, in quotes.

steps.instruction: You can join a String to any other type.
steps.output:
Ada is level 7
Health 2.5, online true
body: The number, the decimal and the boolean are all turned into text and joined on.
This is why every card in this unit was printed with a +.
steps.keypoint: A String can be joined to any other type.

steps.instruction: Ask for a first and last name, then print them joined with a space.
steps.code:
// ask "First? " and "Last? " with readLine
// print them as one line:  Ada Lovelace
steps.target:
First? Ada
Last? Lovelace
Ada Lovelace
steps.hint: Join with + and put a space in the middle.
steps.after: The space had to be its own piece of text.
skills: join Strings together with +

steps.instruction: Here is the bad way to compare them.
body: Both hold the word mellon, and == says false.
It fails because String is not a primitive type.
steps.keypoint: == does not compare the text of a String.

steps.instruction: Here is the good way.

points.label: .equals(b)
points.text: Tests whether the two hold the same characters.

steps.keypoint: .equals() tests whether two Strings hold the same characters.

steps.instruction: Why the two give different answers.
body: Every object is kept somewhere in the computer memory.
On objects, == asks whether the two names point at the same place.
.equals() ignores where they are kept and compares the characters directly.
For int, double, char and boolean there is no place to compare. == looks at the value itself, which is why it works on those.
steps.keypoint: On objects == asks whether two names point at the same place in memory. .equals() compares the characters.

steps.instruction: So the rule is short.

rules.text: Compare text with .equals()
Compare primitives with ==

steps.instruction: Three ways a program goes wrong, and only one of them is loud.

points.label: it will not compile
points.text: A missing semicolon or a misspelt name. Java refuses to run it at all.

points.label: it crashes while running
points.text: It compiles fine, then dies partway - dividing by zero, or asking for character 9 of a 4-letter word.

points.label: it runs and is wrong
points.text: No error at all. It just prints the wrong number, and only you can catch it.

points.label: which is worst
points.text: The last one. The other two tell you where to look.

steps.instruction: A compile error stops it before it starts.

points.label: the missing semicolon
points.text: Line 2 does not end. Java cannot tell where the statement stops.

points.label: no output at all
points.text: Not one line runs. There is nothing to run until it compiles.

points.label: reading the error
points.text: It names a line number. Look at that line and the one above it.

steps.instruction: A run-time error compiles, then dies partway.

points.label: "before" prints
points.text: The program really does start. The first line works.

points.label: 10 / hits
points.text: hits is 0, and integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException.

points.label: "after" never prints
points.text: The crash stops everything from that point.

points.label: hits != 0 &&
points.text: Guard it with short-circuiting, from 3.13.

steps.instruction: Match each mistake to what Java does about it.
pairs: no error at all, just a wrong answer
steps.why: Only the first two are exceptions. The third never starts, and the fourth finishes and lies to you.
skills: name the exception a crash throws

steps.instruction: Run-time crashes have names, and the test asks for them.

points.label: ArithmeticException
points.text: Thrown by integer division by zero: 10 / 0.

points.label: IndexOutOfBoundsException
points.text: Thrown by asking for a position that is not there: "hello".charAt(10) when the last position is 4.

points.label: a compile error has no exception
points.text: A missing semicolon never runs, so nothing is thrown. Exceptions only happen to programs that started.

points.label: reading the name
points.text: The exception name tells you what went wrong before you read a single line of your code.

steps.instruction: Which kind of error is each one?

items.text: a loop that runs one time too few

steps.why: Compile errors are caught before running. Run-time errors stop it partway. Logic errors finish and lie to you.

steps.instruction: A logic error is silent. It just gives the wrong answer.

points.label: expected 5
points.text: The average of 8 and 2 is 5. This prints 9.

points.label: x + y / 2
points.text: Division happens before addition, so it is 8 + 1, not (8 + 2) / 2.

points.label: no error
points.text: It compiled, it ran, it printed a number. Nothing warned you.

points.label: (x + y) / 2
points.text: Brackets force the addition to happen first.
