steps.after: A logic error nothing could have warned you about. Only checking the answer finds these.
skills: tell compile, run-time and logic errors apart

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: String hello = "hello";

questions.prompt: int x = 3 (no semicolon), then int y = 4; then int sum = x + y; — run-time error, compile error, both, or neither?
questions.why: Java cannot tell where the first statement ends, so it refuses to build the program. Nothing runs, so there is no run-time error to have.

questions.prompt: String hello = "hello"; char last = hello.charAt(10); — which exception?
questions.why: "hello" has 5 characters, at positions 0 to 4. Position 10 is outside the String, and that is exactly what this exception means.

skills: name the exception a crash throws

steps.instruction: Two bugs, both stopping it compiling. Hunt them.
steps.hint: A String needs double quotes, and every statement needs a semicolon.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 4.7.5, Bug Hunter, in miniature - single quotes on a String, and a missing semicolon.
skills: tell compile, run-time and logic errors apart

lessons.title: String Processing
objectives: build up a String inside a loop
loop over characters and decide something about all of them

steps.instruction: Most String problems are the same problem wearing a different hat.
body: Build a new String out of an old one, one character at a time.
The hard part is never the syntax. It is knowing the plan before you start typing.
steps.keypoint: Most String problems are: build a new String from an old one, one character at a time.

steps.instruction: Pseudocode is the plan, written in plain words.
body: You write it before the code, not instead of it.
It is not Java, so nothing has to compile and nothing has to be spelled right.

rules.text: create a result string
for every char in the string
do something with the current char
return the result

steps.keypoint: The plan for most String work: make a result, loop every char, do something, return the result.

steps.instruction: Here is that plan as real code. It copies the String character by character.
body: On its own it does nothing useful. It is the frame every exercise below hangs on.
Change the one line in the middle and you change the whole problem.
steps.keypoint: result = result + c inside the loop is how a new String gets built up.

steps.instruction: Step through it and watch result grow.

frames.note: result starts empty. It has to exist before the loop, or every pass would wipe it.
c is the character at 0, which is c.
i++ makes i 3. Not less than 3, so the loop ends.

steps.instruction: Three places a line can go, and it matters which.
body: Putting result = "" inside the loop is the commonest mistake in this lesson. It empties on every pass.
steps.keypoint: Make the result before the loop, decide inside it, return after it.

steps.instruction: This should print gold and prints d. Tap the line to blame.
steps.why: result is made fresh on every pass, so it is emptied each time round and only ever holds the newest character. It has to be made once, before the loop.
skills: build up a String inside a loop

steps.instruction: Worked example: keep only the letters.
body: TASK. Given "a1b2c3", give back "abc".
PLAN. Make a result. For every char, if it is a letter, add it. Return the result.
Only the middle line changed from the frame.

steps.instruction: Worked example: reverse it.
body: TASK. Given "gold", give back "dlog".
PLAN. Make a result. For every char, put it in FRONT of the result. Return the result.
Same frame again. The only change is which side the character goes on.
steps.keypoint: c + result builds backwards. result + c builds forwards.

steps.instruction: Count the vowels in a word.
plan: make a counter, starting at 0
for every char in the word
if the char is a vowel, add one to the counter
print the counter
steps.code:
String s = "programming";
// print how many vowels there are
steps.hint: "aeiou".indexOf(c) gives -1 when c is not a vowel. That is a shorter test than five comparisons.
steps.after: o, a and i. Using indexOf on a String of vowels beats writing c == 'a' || c == 'e' four more times.
skills: loop over characters and decide something about all of them

steps.instruction: Double every vowel. doubleVowel("hello") gives "heelloo".
plan: make an empty result string
for every char in the word
add the char to the result
if it is a vowel, add it a second time
print the result
steps.code:
String s = "hello";
// print heelloo
steps.hint: Add it once always, then a second time only if it is a vowel.
steps.after: Adding unconditionally first, then conditionally, avoids writing the add twice in an if and an else.
skills: build up a String inside a loop

steps.instruction: Write toUpperCase yourself. You may use Character methods but not the String one.
plan: make an empty result string
for every char in the word
turn that char into its capital
add it to the result
print the result
steps.code:
String s = "hello world";
// print HELLO WORLD without using s.toUpperCase()
steps.hint: Character.toUpperCase leaves anything that is not a letter alone, so the space needs no special case.
steps.after: The space came through untouched, because Character.toUpperCase returns anything non-alphabetic unchanged.
skills: build up a String inside a loop

steps.instruction: Are all the letters in the word the same letter?
plan: take the first char as the one to match
for every char in the word
if any char is different, the answer is false
print the answer
steps.code:
String s = "aaaa";
// print true when every character is the same, false otherwise
steps.hint: Start with same = true and only ever set it to false. One difference is enough to settle it.
steps.after: Assume true, then look for a counter-example. That shape solves a whole family of "are they all" questions.
skills: loop over characters and decide something about all of them

steps.instruction: Print the word in AltCase. HeLlO. The first letter is a capital and it alternates from there.
plan: make an empty result string
for every position in the word
if the position is even, add the capital
otherwise add the small letter
print the result
steps.code:
String s = "hello world";
// print HeLlO WoRlD
steps.hint: The position decides, not the character. i % 2 == 0 is every even position.
steps.after: The space counts as a position, which is why the D comes out capital. Using i rather than a counter you manage yourself is what makes this short.
skills: build up a String inside a loop

steps.instruction: Is the word a palindrome? Does it read the same backwards?
plan: make an empty reversed string
for every char in the word, put it in front of the reversed string
compare the reversed string with the original
print the answer
steps.code:
String s = "racecar";
// print true when it reads the same backwards
steps.hint: Build the reverse with c + result, then compare with .equals() and not ==.
steps.after: Reversing then comparing is the plainest solution. Comparing from both ends inwards is faster, but this one is easier to get right.
skills: loop over characters and decide something about all of them

steps.instruction: Do the curly brackets match? {{}} matches. {{} does not.
plan: keep a count of how many brackets are still open
for every char in the string
add one when it opens, take one away when it closes
if the count ever goes below zero, they do not match
at the end they match only if the count is exactly zero
steps.code:
String s = "{{}{{}}}";
// print true when the brackets match, false when they do not
steps.hint: One counter is enough. Going below zero means a closing bracket arrived with nothing to close.
steps.after: Two conditions, both needed. Never going negative means nothing closed too early, and ending at zero means nothing was left open. The empty string gives true, which is correct.
skills: loop over characters and decide something about all of them

steps.instruction: Fix the Sum String. sumString(6, 10) should give "6 + 10 = 16" and currently gives "6 + 10 = 610".
plan: work out the sum as a number first
build the text from the two numbers
add the sum on at the end, in brackets so it stays a number
return the finished string
steps.hint: By the time Java reaches one + two it is already building text, so it glues instead of adding.
steps.after: + adds numbers and joins text, and Java works left to right. Once one side is a String, everything after it is joining. The brackets force the addition to happen first.
skills: build up a String inside a loop

steps.instruction: Ask for a sentence, then print it with every vowel removed.
plan: read the sentence
make an empty result string
for every char in the sentence
if it is not a vowel, add it to the result
print the result
steps.code:
// ask "Sentence? " with readLine
// print it back with a e i o u removed
steps.target:
Sentence? the quick brown fox
th qck brwn fx
steps.hint: Same frame as always. The only new part is that the test is now == -1 instead of != -1.
steps.after: That is the whole lesson in one exercise: read, make a result, loop, decide, print. You now have the shape for any of these.
skills: build up a String inside a loop
loop over characters and decide something about all of them

lessons.title: Methods Quiz
objectives: write a method that returns a value
loop through the characters of a String

steps.instruction: Nothing new. Seven checks across the whole unit.

points.label: what it covers
points.text: Methods, parameters, return values, Javadocs, String methods, characters and errors.

points.label: how to use it
points.text: If one goes wrong, the lesson it came from is the one to reopen.

steps.instruction: What prints?
steps.why: toUpperCase RETURNS a new String and changes nothing. The returned value was never caught, so it was thrown away. A String can never be modified in place - you have to assign the result: s = s.toUpperCase();
skills: write a method that returns a value
use String methods to inspect text

steps.instruction: Which sentence comes out?
steps.why: Arguments fill parameters left to right: "cellar" goes into room, 3 into exits. Position decides, not meaning.
skills: tell an argument apart from a parameter

steps.instruction: Two on Strings.
steps.code: String word = "dungeon";

questions.prompt: What is word.substring(0, 3)?
questions.why: From 0 up to but NOT including 3, so positions 0, 1, 2 - "dun". The end index is always excluded, which is why end - start is the length you get.

questions.prompt: word.charAt(7) does what?
questions.why: "dungeon" has 7 characters at positions 0 to 6. Position 7 does not exist, so it throws at run time - it compiles fine, because Java cannot know the index in advance.

skills: count positions from zero
use String methods to inspect text

steps.instruction: Which kind of error is each one?

items.text: Passing an int where a String parameter is declared
Dividing by a variable that happens to be 0
Averaging by dividing by 2 when there are 3 numbers

steps.why: A compile error stops it before it starts. A run-time error compiles and then dies partway. A logic error does neither - it runs happily and gives you the wrong answer, which is why it is the hardest of the three to find.
skills: tell compile, run-time and logic errors apart

steps.instruction: This method hands a number back. Complete it.
steps.hint: The type on the left says what comes back, and one keyword actually hands it over.
steps.after: void would refuse to return anything, and without return the value is worked out and dropped.
skills: write a method that returns a value

steps.instruction: Write a method that takes a name and hands back a greeting.
steps.hint: run() prints the result, so greet must return a String rather than print one itself.
steps.after: Returning rather than printing is what lets the caller decide what to do with it.
skills: write a method that returns a value
write a method that takes a parameter

steps.instruction: Count the capital letters.
steps.hint: Walk every position with charAt, and ask Character about each one.
steps.after: A and L. The loop plus a counter is the shape behind almost every String question on the test.
skills: loop through the characters of a String
use Character methods to test a character

lessons.title: Introduction to Classes and Objects
objectives: create an object from a class
call a method on an object

steps.instruction: Two monsters already need four loose variables.

points.label: four variables
points.text: goblinName, goblinHp, trollName, trollHp. A third monster makes six.

points.label: nothing ties them
points.text: Java has no idea goblinName and goblinHp belong to the same creature. You just named them carefully.

points.label: the roar is copied
points.text: The sentence is written twice, once per monster.

points.label: what we want
points.text: One thing that holds a name AND its hp AND knows how to roar.

steps.instruction: A class is the blueprint. An object is one thing built from it.

points.label: class Monster
points.text: The blueprint. It says every monster has a name and hp, and knows how to roar.

points.label: new Monster("Goblin", 20)
points.text: Builds ONE monster from that blueprint, with those values.

points.label: Monster goblin =
points.text: The variable holds that object. Its type is Monster, the class name.

points.label: goblin.roar()
points.text: Asks that object to do something. The dot means "belonging to this object".

steps.instruction: Same two monsters. One version keeps them together.

sides.label: loose variables
objects

points.label: loose variables
points.text: Four variables and a copied sentence. A third monster adds two more variables and another copy.

points.label: objects
points.text: Two objects, one blueprint. A third monster is one more line.

skills: create an object from a class

steps.instruction: Each new makes a separate object with its own values.

points.label: two news
points.text: Two objects. goblin and troll are different things built from the same blueprint.

points.label: their own name
points.text: Each object keeps its own name and hp. Changing one does not touch the other.

points.label: one roar method
points.text: Written once in the class, used by both. That is the copied sentence gone.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: getHp() hands back each object's own number, 20 and 45, and + adds them because both are ints.
skills: call a method on an object

steps.instruction: object.method() asks that object to do something.

points.label: goblin.roar()
points.text: Runs roar() for the goblin, using the goblin's name.

points.label: troll.roar()
points.text: Same method, different object, different output.

points.label: goblin.getHp()
points.text: Hands back that object's hp. It returns a value, so you can print or add it.

points.label: the dot
points.text: Reads as "belonging to". Without an object in front, Java does not know whose name to use.

steps.instruction: Build one more monster and make it roar.
steps.hint: new builds the object. A dot reaches into it.
steps.after: new to build, dot to ask. Those two do most of the work in this unit.
skills: create an object from a class

steps.instruction: One word is missing, and without it Java looks for a method.
steps.hint: A constructor is never called on its own. Something has to ask for the object to be built.
steps.after: new is what actually makes the object. Without it Java reads Monster(...) as a call to a method named Monster, and there is no such method.
skills: create an object from a class

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: Monster goblin = new Monster("Goblin", 20);

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between a class and an object?
opts: A class is a blueprint; an object is one thing built from it
An object is a blueprint; a class is built from it
questions.why: One class can produce any number of objects, each with its own values. The class itself holds no values.

questions.prompt: In goblin.roar(), what does the dot mean?
opts: roar() belongs to the goblin object
questions.why: The dot reaches into a specific object and asks it to run one of its methods.

skills: call a method on an object

steps.instruction: Your turn: make two monsters, roar both, then print their combined hp.
steps.hint: Two new Monster(...) lines, then bat.roar(); dragon.roar(); then println(bat.getHp() + dragon.getHp());
steps.after: You used a class someone else wrote without changing a line of it. Writing your own comes in 5.4.
skills: create an object from a class

lessons.title: Classes vs. Objects
objectives: tell a class apart from an object
call methods that change an object's state

steps.instruction: Every object holds two things: what it IS, and what it can DO.
steps.output:
Goblin has 20 hp
Goblin roars!
Goblin has 15 hp

points.label: state
points.text: name and hp. The values this particular monster is carrying right now.

points.label: behaviour
points.text: roar() and takeDamage(). The things it knows how to do.

points.label: 20 then 15
points.text: takeDamage changed the state. Same object, different values.

points.label: an object
points.text: is exactly those two things bundled together, which loose variables never were.

steps.instruction: Class or object?
steps.why: A class is the template and there is one of it. An object is a thing built from it, and there can be any number.
skills: tell a class apart from an object

steps.instruction: "Instance" is just another word for object.

points.label: class Monster
points.text: The template. Written once.

points.label: goblin
points.text: An object. Also called an instance of Monster. The two words mean the same thing.

points.label: "instantiate"
points.text: The verb for building one: new Monster(...) instantiates the class.

points.label: why two words
points.text: Exam questions use both. Nothing more to it than that.

steps.instruction: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the template a thing is built from
one thing built from a template
the values an object is holding
the methods an object can run
steps.why: Class is the template; object and instance both mean one thing made from it; state and behaviour are the two halves it carries.
skills: tell a class apart from an object

steps.instruction: Each object keeps its own state.

points.label: goblin.takeDamage(5)
points.text: Only the goblin was hit. Its hp fell from 20 to 15.

points.label: troll.getHp()
points.text: Still 45. The troll was never touched.

points.label: one class
points.text: Both were built from Monster, and both have their own separate name and hp.

points.label: the method is shared
points.text: takeDamage exists once, in the class. Which object it changes depends on the dot.

steps.instruction: The goblin is hit twice. What prints?
steps.why: Each call changes the same object's hp: 20 - 5 is 15, then 15 - 3 is 12. The changes accumulate because it is one object.
skills: call methods that change an object's state

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code: Monster goblin = new Monster("Goblin", 20);

questions.prompt: An object has both...
questions.why: State is the values it holds; behaviour is the methods it can run. That pairing is the definition.

questions.prompt: Which is a class, and which is an object?
opts: Monster is the class, goblin is the object
goblin is the class, Monster is the object
questions.why: Monster is the template. goblin is one thing built from it.

skills: tell a class apart from an object

steps.instruction: Your turn: hit one of two monsters and show both are separate.
steps.hint: Two new Monster lines, then bat.takeDamage(3);, then print bat.getHp() and dragon.getHp().
steps.after: The dragon is untouched at 200. Separate objects, separate state.
skills: call methods that change an object's state

lessons.title: Using a Class as a Client
objectives: use a class from its documentation alone

steps.instruction: You have never written the Monster class. You did not need to.

points.label: a client
points.text: Code that USES a class without being the class. That is what your run() has been all along.

points.label: why it matters
points.text: You can use String, Scanner and Math without reading a line of their source. Same idea, smaller class.

points.label: what you need
points.text: Not the code - just the list of methods, what they take, and what they give back.

points.label: where that lives
points.text: In the Javadoc, which is why 4.4 spent a lesson on writing them.

steps.instruction: This is all a client is given.

points.label: the comment block
points.text: Five lines telling you everything you can do with a Monster.

points.label: Monster(String, int)
points.text: The constructor: what to pass to new.

points.label: int getHp()
points.text: int on the left means it hands back a number, so it can go in a println.

points.label: void roar()
points.text: void means nothing comes back. Calling it in a println would not compile.

steps.instruction: From the docs above: which method gives you a number to print?
steps.hint: println needs a value. Which of the three returns one rather than void?
steps.after: roar() and takeDamage() are void - they do something. getHp() answers something.
skills: use a class from its documentation alone

steps.instruction: The docs say roar() is void. This does not compile.
steps.hint: void means nothing comes back, so there is nothing for println to print. roar already prints for itself.
steps.after: A void method is a whole statement on its own. Only a method with a type on the left can go inside println.
skills: use a class from its documentation alone

steps.instruction: One line asks for something the documentation never offered. Tap it.
steps.why: The docs list roar, takeDamage, getHp and getName. There is no setHp, so hp can only go DOWN through takeDamage. As a client the documentation is all you get - if it is not listed, you cannot call it.
skills: use a class from its documentation alone

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.
steps.code:
// int getHp()
// void roar()

questions.prompt: What does it mean to be a client of a class?
opts: To copy the class into your file
To use the class without writing or changing it
questions.why: A client calls the methods. Someone else owns the implementation.

questions.prompt: Why can you use a class without reading its source?
opts: The documentation says what each method takes and returns
questions.why: The method list is the contract. How it works inside is not your problem, and can change without breaking you.

skills: use a class from its documentation alone

steps.instruction: Your turn: use the documented methods only.
steps.hint: new Monster("Slime", 12), then .roar(), then .takeDamage(4), then println(.getHp()).
steps.after: You wrote that from a five-line comment. You still have not read the class.
skills: use a class from its documentation alone

lessons.title: Writing Classes
objectives: write a class with private instance variables and a constructor
write a toString so the object can be printed

steps.instruction: You have used Monster for three lessons. Now build your own.

points.label: Treasure
points.text: A chest item with a name and a value in gold.

points.label: what it needs
points.text: Somewhere to keep those two values, and a way to build one.

points.label: the client is written
points.text: run() already makes a Crown worth 120 and prints it. Your job is the class it needs.

steps.instruction: A class has fields, then a constructor.

points.label: private String name;
points.text: An instance variable. Every Treasure gets its own copy of this.

points.label: private
points.text: Only code inside Treasure can touch it. The client cannot reach in.

points.label: public Treasure(String name, int value)
points.text: The constructor. Same name as the class, and no return type at all.

points.label: this.name = name;
points.text: this.name is the field; name is the parameter. Without this. you would assign the parameter to itself.

steps.instruction: println(object) calls toString().

points.label: public String toString()
points.text: Spelled exactly like that. Java looks for this name.

points.label: System.out.println(crown)
points.text: No .toString() written anywhere, and yet it runs. println asks the object for its String.

points.label: without it
points.text: You would get Treasure@1b6d3586 - the class name and a memory address.

steps.instruction: Two treasures, one class. What prints?
steps.why: Each object holds its own name and value, and toString uses whichever object it was called on.
skills: write a class with private instance variables and a constructor

steps.instruction: The constructor forgot something. Fix it.
steps.hint: name = name assigns the parameter to itself. The field needs this. in front.
steps.after: Without this., the fields stay null and 0 - which is why it printed "null (0 gold)".
skills: write a class with private instance variables and a constructor

steps.instruction: This was meant to be a constructor. One line stops it being one. Tap it.
steps.why: A constructor has NO return type at all. Adding void turns it into an ordinary method that merely happens to be called Treasure, so the class keeps only the automatic no-argument constructor and new Treasure("Crown") will not compile.
skills: write a class with private instance variables and a constructor

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.

questions.prompt: What is different about a constructor?
opts: It can only take one parameter
It has the class name and no return type
questions.why: Same name as the class, and no type before the name - not even void.

questions.prompt: Why write toString()?
opts: So printing the object shows something readable
So the object can be created
questions.why: println looks for toString(). Without one you get the class name and a memory address.

skills: write a toString so the object can be printed

steps.instruction: Your turn: write the Potion class the client needs.
steps.code:
// write class Potion with a private name and healing, a constructor,
// and a toString returning e.g. "Small Potion heals 20"
steps.target:
Small Potion heals 20
Large Potion heals 75
steps.hint: Two private fields, a constructor using this., and public String toString() returning name + " heals " + healing.
steps.after: You wrote a class and the client used it unchanged. That is both sides of 5.3 now.
skills: write a class with private instance variables and a constructor

lessons.title: Writing Classes and Instance Methods
objectives: write instance methods that use and change the fields
tell an instance variable apart from an instance method

steps.instruction: Treasure can be printed. It cannot do anything.

points.label: what it has
points.text: name and value. Instance variables - its state.

points.label: what it does
points.text: Nothing yet, apart from describe itself.

points.label: what we want
points.text: polish() to raise its value, and isRare() to answer a question about it.

steps.instruction: An instance method can use the fields directly.

points.label: public void polish()
points.text: An instance method. No static, so it belongs to one object.

points.label: value = value + 10;
points.text: No dot, no parameter. Inside the class, the fields are just there.

points.label: crown.polish()
points.text: Runs it for the crown, so the crown's value changes and nothing else does.

points.label: 95 then 105
points.text: The same object printed twice, with a changed field in between.

steps.instruction: Data only, or data that can act.

sides.label: client does the work
object does the work

points.label: client does the work
points.text: Every client must know that polishing means +10. Change the rule and you change every client.

points.label: object does the work
points.text: The rule lives in the class. Clients just ask.

skills: write instance methods that use and change the fields

steps.instruction: An instance method can answer a question too.

points.label: public boolean isRare()
points.text: Returns a value, so it can go in a println or an if.

points.label: return value > 100;
points.text: Uses the object's own value. The crown is 120, the ring is 45.

points.label: same method, two answers
points.text: Which object you call it on decides the result.

steps.instruction: Instance variable, or instance method?
steps.why: Variables hold state and have a type and a name. Methods have brackets and a body.
skills: tell an instance variable apart from an instance method

steps.instruction: Only one of them gets polished. What prints?
steps.why: polish() ran on a. Each object has its own value, so the ring never heard about it. That is what "belongs to one object" means.
skills: write instance methods that use and change the fields

steps.instruction: isRare works out the answer and then loses it.
steps.hint: The comparison happens, but nothing hands the answer back to whoever called it.
steps.after: A method with a type on the left MUST return that type. Working the answer out is not the same as giving it back.
skills: write instance methods that use and change the fields

steps.instruction: Two the test asks.

questions.prompt: Why does polish() not need value as a parameter?
opts: It is a field of the same object, so it is already in scope
questions.why: An instance method runs on one object and can see that object's fields by name.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an instance variable and an instance method?
opts: A variable is private; a method is public
A variable is what the object has; a method is what it does
questions.why: State versus behaviour - the same pair from 5.2.

skills: tell an instance variable apart from an instance method

steps.instruction: Your turn: give Potion a drink() and a isStrong().
steps.code:
// class Potion: private name and healing, a constructor,
// drink() halves healing, isStrong() returns healing > 50
steps.hint: drink() sets healing = healing / 2. isStrong() returns healing > 50. Neither takes a parameter.

points.text: Runs when you pass two arguments.

points.label: Potion(String)
points.text: Runs when you pass one, and fills in 10 itself.

one overloaded name

whether it is the same object

Take the 8, take the 4, skip the 2, take the 1.

lessons.title: Ethical Issues Around Data Collection
objectives: judge whether a data practice needs consent
explain how combining fields reveals more than any one field

steps.instruction: A step counter needs your steps. Look at what it actually takes.

points.label: what it needs
points.text: A step count. That is the whole product.

points.label: what it takes
points.text: Location every few minutes, so it can measure distance.

points.label: and keeps
points.text: Timestamps. When you left, when you got back, every day for two years.

points.label: the gap
points.text: Nothing here is stolen. Every field has a reason. The reasons are not the problem.

steps.instruction: One field is boring. Fields together are not.

points.label: a location
points.text: A point on a map. Could be anyone.

points.label: locations at 3am, every night
points.text: Where you sleep. That is your home address.

points.label: plus 9am on weekdays
points.text: Your school or your workplace.

points.label: aggregation
points.text: The conclusion was never in any single row. It came from putting rows side by side.

steps.instruction: "We remove your name" does less than it sounds.

points.label: the claim
points.text: The name column is deleted, so the data is anonymous.

points.label: ZIP code, date of birth, sex
points.text: Three fields nobody thinks twice about. Together they narrow most people down to a single person.

points.label: re-identification
points.text: Match those three against any public list that does have names, and the name is back.

points.label: anonymous is relative
points.text: Anonymous is not a property of one table. It depends on every other table that exists.

steps.instruction: Sort each one.

items.text: The step counter stores your steps so you can see last week
It keeps your location history to measure distance walked
It sells that location history to an advertiser
It uses your data to improve its step-counting accuracy
It shares data with a research hospital, with names removed
It keeps your full history after you delete your account

steps.why: The line is rarely the data itself. It is whether the use is the one you agreed to, and whether you could say no.
skills: judge whether a data practice needs consent

steps.instruction: Match each term to what it means.
pairs: Combining separate fields to learn something no single field said
Putting names back onto data that had them removed
Collecting only the fields the feature actually needs
Off until the user turns it on
On until the user finds the setting and turns it off
steps.why: Opt-in and opt-out collect the same field. They differ only in who has to act, and that decides what most people end up with.
skills: judge whether a data practice needs consent

steps.instruction: Two worth being sure about.

questions.prompt: An app collects your contacts to "improve your experience". What is the strongest objection?
opts: It should be opt-out instead of opt-in
The purpose is too vague to agree or disagree with
Contacts are never useful to an app
questions.why: You cannot consent to a purpose you cannot picture. A reason that covers everything is not a reason.

questions.prompt: A dataset has no names, but has ZIP, birth date and sex. Is it anonymous?
opts: No - those three together often identify one person
Only if it has fewer than 1000 rows
Yes, as long as it is not made public
questions.why: That is exactly the combination re-identification attacks use.

skills: judge whether a data practice needs consent

steps.instruction: The step counter shows steps per day, and nothing else. Which fields does it need to KEEP?

items.text: How many steps you took each day
Which account the steps belong to
Your exact GPS path for every walk
The wifi networks your phone saw on the way
The time of every single step, kept for two years

steps.why: Distance can be measured and then thrown away - the daily total is what the feature shows. Data minimisation is this exact question asked field by field, and what you never keep cannot leak.
skills: judge whether a data practice needs consent

steps.prompt: A school app records which websites each student visits during class, so teachers can see who is off task. Name one thing about it you think is reasonable, and one change you would require before it ships.
steps.rubric: Credit an answer that (a) acknowledges a legitimate purpose - the teacher does have a reason to know whether students are working - and (b) names a concrete, specific change rather than a general objection. Strong changes: limit it to class time only, show teachers a status rather than a full browsing list, delete the logs after a set period, tell students plainly that it is on, collect only whether a site is on-task rather than which site. Weak answers reject it outright with no purpose acknowledged, or ask vaguely for "more privacy" with nothing specific.
skills: judge whether a data practice needs consent
steps.instruction: Write a few sentences. There is no single right answer here.
Four questions to ask about any feature you build.

points.label: What does it need?
points.text: Not what would be useful. What breaks if you leave the field out.

points.label: How long?
points.text: Data kept forever is data that leaks eventually.

points.label: Who else sees it?
points.text: Every extra copy is another place it can go wrong.

points.label: Could they say no?
points.text: And still use the thing. If not, it was not really a choice.

steps.instruction: Which structure fits each job?

items.text: Exactly 7 daily temperatures, count never changes
A queue of students that grows and shrinks all day
Look a phone number up by a person's name
Count how many times each word appears in a book

steps.why: Fixed count means an array. Changing count means an ArrayList. Looking up BY something other than position means a map. A grid means two dimensions.
skills: choose the right structure for a job
